column1: # scenarios.tsv
# ReixOS
# The QEMU boot matrix, as data. scripts/scenarios.sh reads this file and boots
# one row at a time through scripts/smoke.sh, so a new machine configuration is
# a new line here rather than a new script or a new Makefile target.
# Tab-separated, ten columns, `-` for a column that does not apply. Blank lines
# and `#` lines are ignored. A field may contain spaces; it may not contain a
# tab, and runs of tabs collapse, so every column needs its placeholder.
#   id         row name: its serial log lands in .reix/scenario-<id>.log
#   mem        guest RAM, e.g. `4M` (`-` = the machine default)
#   initrd     `qemu` (handed over with -initrd) or `embedded` (the copy the
#              plugin links into kernel.bin under `.initrd`)
#   flags      QEMU flags appended after the base set (`-` = none). Appended and
#              not merged: QEMU keeps the last `-cpu`/`-machine` it is given, so
#              a row overrides one of them without restating the whole machine.
#   mode       `verdict` stops the guest at the first success/failure marker,
#              exactly like `make smoke`. `window` keeps it running for the full
#              timeout and judges the log afterwards, which is what a row needs
#              when it asserts lines printed after the success marker.
#              `typed:<text>` is `window` plus a typist: the text is written to
#              the guest's serial port, `\n` for a newline, and the serial port
#              stays on stdio so the log still comes back through the engine.
#   timeout    seconds: the deadline under `verdict`, the run length under `window`
#   required   markers that must all appear, in this order, `|`-separated. The
#              order is a subsequence, not adjacency: other lines may sit
#              between two markers, and each marker only has to appear after
#              the line that satisfied the previous one.
#   forbidden  markers that must not appear anywhere, `|`-separated (`-` = none)
#              Every row that types nothing forbids the shell's parting line: with
#              no command typed, a shell that stopped reading stopped on its own.
#              The `typed:` rows are the exception, and they require it instead.
#   post       extra check run after the markers hold (`-` = none). The names are
#              the post_* functions in scripts/scenarios.sh.
#   expect     `pass`, `xfail:<reason>`, or `skip-if:<condition>`
# On the marker sets, both of which are deliberately narrow:
#   * A healthy boot prints no `[ ERROR ]` line at all, verified against every
#     configuration below, so the level tag itself is forbidden rather than any
#     particular message. A panic is caught twice: `[ PANIC ]` is the level tag
#     and `REIX-PANIC` is the report banner, which the nested-fault path prints
#     without a level tag.
#   * Only single-writer lines are required. The kernel's `[ INFO  ][ELF ]`
#     spawn lines interleave with userland output and shred whatever line they
#     land in the middle of, so nothing printed during a spawn is asserted -
#     including the initrd page-sharing line, which is the one that shreds.
# id
# The configuration `make smoke` boots: machine default RAM, initrd from QEMU.
# The required chain is one boot read end to end - the pre-Swift banner, the
# subsystems in bring-up order, the handoff to EL0, init, and finally the
# VT adapter, which is the last thing init starts that announces itself and
# so the latest single-writer line every configuration here prints.
default

column1: # The guard on smoke-4m's coupling: at 4 MiB, MEM and INITRD_MODE are one knob
# and not two, because QEMU drops an -initrd halfway up RAM and then 2 MiB-aligns
# the generated DTB after it, which lands past the top of the machine. QEMU says
# exactly that and exits before the kernel runs, so its message is what this row
# requires and the success marker is what it forbids.
# Which makes this row failing good news rather than a regression: it would mean
# the guest booted all the way through on `qemu` at 4 MiB, INITRD_MODE=embedded
# stopped being load-bearing, and the coupling can be relaxed - in `smoke-4m` and
# `run-4m` in the Makefile, and in the mem-4m row above.
dtb-squeeze

column1: # The storage stack, end to end, in one row: the bus walks the transports and
# carves a window and a line, gives both to a driver and drops its own copies,
# the driver hands its endpoint back to the bus, the bus reads the sectors while
# it is still the only process that can reach them and then hands the disk to
# init and keeps nothing, init hands it to a file system, the file system claims
# the volume and mounts and gives its one root capability back. Init then cuts a
# container out of that and starts a process inside that container and nothing
# else. That process proves three things: that it can use its own room, that it
# cannot reach a single object outside it even by naming numbers it was never
# told, and that the two ways of receiving something from another container both
# work and agree - a read-only capability naming one file, and a pipe carrying
# the same bytes with nothing else attached to them.
# `window` because all of it happens after the success marker.
# The post-check reads the virtqueue's memory barriers out of the linked driver.
# A barrier has no result to compare and its absence shows up as a race on
# hardware nobody here runs, so what is checkable is that the instructions exist,
# that they name the outer-shareable domain the device is in rather than the
# inner one the console ring uses, and that the queue submission still reaches
# them. It catches deletion and inlining, and claims no more than that.
# Every failure any of those four can report is forbidden by name. A stack this
# deep has too many ways to stop quietly for a missing marker to be a diagnosis.
# `[ FS    ] mounted` is required now that the handoff is a handover rather than
# a lookup: the bus finishes reading before init is told the disk exists, so the
# order of these lines is the order the capability travelled in and not a race.
# The forbidden line about what a finished write achieves is how this row asserts
# that QEMU's virtio-blk still negotiates `VIRTIO_BLK_F_FLUSH`. A device that did
# not would report no durability at all, and the file system refuses to mount one
# of those rather than guessing - so its absence is the negotiation succeeding,
# named rather than inferred from the mount marker being there.
# How deep the queue actually got is the `queue-depth` post-check rather than a
# marker: the block server prints it while other processes are printing theirs, so
# where its line lands between somebody else's is a race, and a marker chain is an
# ordered subsequence. See `post_queue_depth` for why the floor is two and not the
# four slots the driver has.
# The forbidden lines starting "the device" are every way a used ring can
# disagree with what was submitted, plus the two ways a size can move under a
# request, plus the one refusal that comes from this side: a wait that could not
# be bounded. None of them is a request failing; each is the device being reset.
# "a completion had nowhere to be recorded" and "this server lost count of what it
# owes" are the block server's own bookkeeping contradicting itself: four slots
# owing more than four answers. It takes the disk out of service, so it is
# forbidden rather than merely noted.
# "the file system refused itself" is the journal's own guard reporting: a change
# to the disk's bookkeeping attempted with no transaction open. No client can
# provoke it, so its appearance would mean a mutation reached the medium without
# going through the journal - or rather, tried to and was stopped.
# The two about checking are the dirty mount's own recovery: a volume it could not
# check is a volume it refuses to serve, and a room walk that did not finish is a
# device that stopped answering. Every boot in this matrix mounts dirty - the
# machine is killed rather than shut down - so both lines are on the path.
storage

column1: # The shell's closing, which is the one thing about it that cannot be shown from
# a host: that `exit` is the end of reading and not a flag somebody remembered to
# test. Two lines are typed. The first is `shell.exit()`, and the parting line
# below is what says it was read - the shell only writes that line because the
# terminal delivered it, the editor closed it, the parser took it apart, and
# CoreModule answered that it had been asked to stop.
# The second typed line is one no module answers to, and both halves of what a
# shell would make of it are forbidden: its echo appearing anywhere means the
# shell read a line after it was told to stop, and `no such receiver` means it
# interpreted one. Neither is in any other output of this machine.
# The echo of the first line is deliberately not required. Every character of an
# echo is its own flush, so a second writer can land between two of them, and the
# rule at the top of this file is that only single-writer lines are asserted. The
# prompt is one flush and is required; the echo is not.
# The guest runs to the end of the window rather than stopping at the parting
# line, because what this row asks about is what came after it. That is the
# post-check's half: nothing at all, and in particular no further prompt, which a
# forbidden marker could not say because the prompt before the exit is legitimate.
shell-exit
